chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
title: No second line at the 1986 parade, versus the 1950s
summary: Wood notes almost no second line at the June 1986 parade and contrasts it with the joyous umbrella-waving kids of the late 1950s.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Well, do you remember the bass drummer with Young Tuxedo that day? Did you talk to him?
I happened to run into him on the street yesterday. And he remembered you being there with your daughter and her friend. He was commenting on the number of second one, I say.
Oh, it wasn't you, your daughter. Okay, it was somebody else himself.

Well, one of my reactions to that parade was that they weren't in the second liners. That the only thing that even came close to it was me and this guy, Carl Peter, somebody from Norway. And he and I walked the whole way from where they started to the end, right along with the Young Tuxedo Band. And every once in a while there'd be a little knot of people on the sidewalk that would kind of get with it a little bit and clap as he went by. But there was basically no second line. And I was very much aware of that. And I noticed, and I wondered if that was because they were going down Canal Street as opposed to going through a residential neighborhood where they might have drawn people into the houses. I remember that. I remember that that was one of the things that used to delight me about going to the Bass Brass Band parades in the late 50s was that whenever the band got assembled and whatever the procession was that they were there for, whether it was a Sunday school parade or a large parade or whether they were playing for a funeral and the funeral group, the club or whatever it was called was assembled. And they would start off that just almost instantaneously. The sidewalks would be full of these really young kids, usually teenage guys with tattered umbrellas and just swooping up and down. They had a little kind of gate step that they did. They went up and down and forward. And it was just marvelous. It was a free, open, sort of joyous, kind of spontaneous thing. And that's why that parade two days ago was really pretty flat in that respect. I mean, they were marching along in the procession of automobiles. You know, they had a whole bunch of convertibles in front of them and behind them containing dignitaries of the church. And nobody heard them except those guys riding in the cars and the occasional person on the sidewalk. It was pretty flat in that respect. And again, to me, it indicates that the brass band tradition as it survives now is really pretty fragile as a phenomenon of the life of the city. That it was just sort of grafted onto that parade. And it really is not, you know, as the sort of part of the fabric of the community that it was 30 years ago, I guess it is.
Well, I know exactly what you're talking about in that case. I'd hate to generalize. Maybe there are things going on that we don't know anymore about.
